"I cannot tell," she shook her head.

"What is music, Mamma dear,
Can YOU give the answer to us here?"

"Probably not," made reply.

The first saw farmer hale and brown,
Who had just come home from a ride;
'What is music?' asked as he came near;
And he answered with laugh that was good:
'What is music? did YOU see
In the hum of those mowers out there cut
Next week twill be the binders on the wheat?'
They make music to me very sweet."

"What is music?" I asked of a tailor.

In a building where fabrics were made fine,
It's the whirr of those looms all day long;
If you listen alright they make quite a song.

"What is music?" asked of miser old;
And he quickly answered 'Tis the rattle of gold;
There is nothing else that can make the same
As turn my beauteous treasure around."

I met a woman, sad, cast down,
Who was loved from black from foot to crown.
"What is music?" softly said;
'Tis the voices of loved ones who now are dead;

On brook's mossy bank one summer's day.

As it trills and ripples on its way to the lakes;
Hear the thrush on yon topmost bough,
It is music made from the sound, now;
Hear the soft rustle of the leaves overhead,
How they dance with one another, by the
South wind led.

I met a lovely, fair young wife,
Who had hardly known a care in life.

Mamma has come, and a moment more
A beautiful boy bounded over the floor.
Her wraps were quickly thrown aside,
She taking her boy with loving pride,
She said: "This is music all day long,

To a dear old saint with whitened head.

Sheriff Nint Anglin and Ben Shaver got

Atterbury and William Shea, charged

twelve miles southeast of here. The
theft took place in Denton county, to
which place the prisoners will be carried.

tory about the finding of a wagon, and
about which there is mystery the peo-
ple are unable to solve. It seems that a
wagon has been standing near public
road on prairie about eight miles from
Lebanon, T., for the past three weeks,
and when examined by parties few days
ago it showed two or three bullet holes,
and had in its trunk in which there was a
bloody shirt. The trunk was unlocked,
and on the inside were the keys. The
wagon was worth about $50, and had in
it a good camping outfit, with provisions
for men and feed for horses, several pair
of good raw-hide hobbles and branding
irons of all descriptions. Two letters
were found in the trunk, but noth-
ing was gleaned from them to identify
the outfit. On the trunk was the
name "Crank Patterson." The property
was taken to Mr. Geo. McMillan's in the
neighborhood. The team to the
wagon was gone and, though diligent
search was made, nothing was found to
enable the parties to solve the mystery.

strange affair, and it is feared that a ter-
rible tragedy has been committed. Leb-
anon is about forty miles northeast of
here.

day while shoeing little Spanish mule.

The following story told of DR. William S. White, formerly chaplain of the University of Virginia. It is one of the best illustrations of quick and apt retort:


When J. L. Orr was Speaker of the House, he spent a short time at Warm Springs, in North Carolina, where DR. White was also. The two had been sitting for some time apart, each engaged with his own knot of immediate friends, and by and by the doctor arose and walked across the room, with the old-time limp in his gait.


Mr. Orr immediately recognized him, and asked him if he were not the chaplain at the University of Virginia at such time, naming the year. The doctor replied that he was.


"I was there," said Mr. Orr, "a student at the time, and I knew you by the peculiar limp of your step."


"Well," said the doctor, a little severely, though with a twinkle which told that he spoke jokingly, "it seems that my limp made a deeper impression on you than my preaching."


"Ah, DOCTOR," quickly replied Mr. Orr, "I deem it the highest compliment we can pay a clergyman to say he is known by his walk rather than by his conversation."


(Charlottesville, Va.) Chronicle.

a tobacco warehouse, and it was crowded
by the planters for miles around. Booth
and his companions had arranged to take
the weekly steamer, expected to call late
at night, and between the acts were busy
packing up. The play was "The Mer-
chant of Venice" and they were just
going on for the trial scene when they
heard a whistle and the manager came
running in to say that the steamer had
arrived and would leave again in ten min
utes. As that was their only chance for
a week of getting away, they were in
terrible quandary.

"They will think they are being
cheated and we shall have free fight.
The only thing is for you fellows to get
up some sort of natural-like impromptu
ending for the piece and ring down the
curtain. Go right ahead, ladies and gen-
tlemen, and take your cue from Ned
here," and he hurried away to get the
luggage aboard.

Ned, of course, was Bassanio, and he
resolved to rely on the ignorance of the
Virginians of those days to pull him
through all right. So when old George
Ruggles, who was doing Shylock, began
to sharpen his knife on his boot Booth
walked straight up to him and solemnly
said

"You are bound to have the flesh, are
you?"

"You bet your life!" said Ruggles.

"Now, I'll make you one more offer"
continued Booth "In addition to this
big bag of ducats I'll throw in two kegs
of niggorbead tobacco, shotgun and
two of the best coon dogs in the State"

"I'm blamed if I don't do it!" re-
sponded Shylock, much to the approba-
tion of the audience, who were tobacco
raisers and coon hunters to a man.

"And to show that there's no ill-feel-
ing, I'll Portia, Gwen wind up with
a Virginiy reel"

When they got on board the steamer
the captain, who had witnessed the con-
clusion of the play, remarked:

"I'd like to see the whole of that play,
gentlemen. I'm blamed if I thought
that fellow Shakespeare had so much
snap in him."

This Is probably owing to the fact that


wild ducks, geese and brants are still


plentiful in most parts of the country.


and hunters supply the market with


birds at lower prices than farmers can


afford to raise them. During the hunt


ing season wild water-fowls are often
cheaper than any article of meat


that can be obtained. The general use


of pork also interferes with the demand


for ducks and geese. The farmer sup


plies all the fat meat that most people


desire to eat. Most of our native popu-


lation prefer turkeys and chickens to


ducks and geese. Till recently most
persons have raised geese chiefly for the
feathers they afford. Most of the geese
that have been sent to market have been
old and tough. More pains have been


taken TO improve chickens designed for
the table than to improve the breed of
geese raised for the same purpose. The
majority of American families who set
fine tables and who study TO obtain a
great variety of food do not have roast
goose oftener than once q year. Geese
in this country are chiefly eaten By per-
sons of foreign birth.


Ii is likely that the home demand for
domesticated ducks and geese will inn
prove as the supply of wild birds de-
creases, as 1t doubtless will in few
years. The number that are slaughter
ed by hunters every spring and fall is
enormous. Many are killed simply for
sport. In the meantime their old nest
ing places in the Northwestern Terrific
ries and Canada are being encroached
on by settlers. We are reminded
by foreign papers that there is fresh
demand for geese abroad. In England,
il appears, every well-regulated family
serves up fat goose at the Feast of ST.
Michael as the American families do
turkey on Thanksgiving day. MANY
families prefer goose 10 chicken or beef
al hristmss. The country no longer
produces geese enough to supply the de-
mand for them. Frozen geese are
brought 10 London and other cities dur
ing the winter season from Russia, Ger
many and Canada. They bring about
sixteen cents per pound. Ireland and
North France also supply dressed geese
at different seasons of the year. As these
have not been frozen. they bring better
prices. Except during warm weather,
when there is no demand for them.
dressed geese can be kept week with
out danger of injury.


Many of the geese eaten in English
cities during the winter come from coun-
tries on the continent, chiefly from Hol-
t,,,& g.
brought over In vessels and are driven
through the country TO farms. where
they are fattended for the market. Most
of these foreign geese are landed at Har-
wick, and are driven into Cambridge
and Norfolk Counties TO be fed. They
suffer from sea-sickness during their
passage and from inconsistencies after
they reach their destination. They also
become very foot-sore during their long
march. They soon become contented,
however. and have an excellent appe-
tite. On account of the condition of
their feet they remain very quiet on
their feeding ground. and lay on fat
much more rapidly than geese that are
constantly moving about. They are
generally fed about five weeks before
they are sent 70 market. Individual
breeders not infrequently purchase and
fatter as many as eight thousand geese
in the course of a year. The breeders
arrange with marketmen In relation 10
the number of geese that shall be sent
at any given time. They are killed.
plucked and nicely packed in baskets or
crates before they are sent 20 market.
Finely-fsttened geese, well dressed, and
not over ten months old, ordinarily
bring a shilling, or twenty-five cents,
per pound during the winter holidays.


There would seem to be little diff
Guilty in sending either live or dressed
geese from this country TO England.
The steamers now make such good time
that during cold weather dressed geese
could be sent from New York TO Liver
pool without danger of injury. Live
geese would suffer less from transpOrta-
ton by rail than live cattle, sheep and
pigs do. A car having four floors or

Hayer, Philadelphia, from Pensacola, Fla., to Philadelphia, twelve days out, 935 miles; "Chimney Bill," owned by C. K. J., from Pensacola to Newark, 1,010 miles, twenty-six days out; "Montgomery," owned by Samuel Hunt, Fall River, from Montgomery, Ala., to Fall River, 1,010 miles, in thirty-nine days. From the above record it will be seen that Mr. Friesmuth's bird has made a remarkably quick trip, breaking the record for long distance flying in a rather bad way. The pigeon came into the loft in excellent shape, and showed little evidence of the tremendous journey it had performed. It trembled very perceptibly, and was hungry, but beyond that seemed to be none the worse for its flight. Mr. Friesmuth was on watch for the pigeon, and the time was noted exactly by watch. A careful examination of the bird showed that two or three feathers were missing from its tail, and a few from its breast, but whether they had been dropped accidentally or lost through some mishap, such as a contact with some bird of prey, cannot be ascertained. The bird is eighteen months old, while the other one, still aloft, is a young bird of but nine months, and therefore not able to make as good time.

Some very remarkable flights of carrier pigeons are on record. Probably the most extraordinary was a trip made from St. Sebastian, Spain, to Liege, Belgium, in 1862. The distance is 615 miles, and sixteen birds being liberated at St. Sebastian in the morning, one arrived at Liege the same night. The sport is very popular in Belgium, arising to the dignity of a national pastime. Every fifth person is a pigeon owner, and a majority of the dwellings have the peculiar dormer window which tells of the pigeon loft beneath the roof. The extent to which the pastime is carried on can be imagined when it is known that in six months of last year more than a million pigeons, occupying eleven hundred and six coops, were sent to France to be liberated from a single Belgian province. The birds are sent away in such numbers that special trains are often run on the railroads to accommodate them. The best time ever made in Europe is a mile in forty-eight seconds, made from Arlos to Antwerp. The distance is 901 miles and it was made by a bird in 30 minutes.

Here in America the sport is but fifteen years old. The first incentive to long distance flying was in 1879 when a reward of 500 was offered for a bird which should cover 500 miles. An attempt to win this, by flying birds from Columbus, O., to New York, resulted in the two pigeons being lost. The next year birds succeeded in flying from Steubenville to New York City, "Francisco" owned by L. Meeterleer, of Hoboken, making the trip in eight hours and eighteen minutes. Since that time the distances have been gradually increased, many flights having been made from the Steubenville Court House, Indianapolis, Columbus, and points in the Southern States, all centering at New York and vicinity, where most of the American birds are owned.

Mr. Friesmuth's long distance bird is a beautiful one, full breasted and well feathered, and yesterday afternoon, after its arrival, it attracted much attention.

and then go for help. Backwards and for-
wards, round and round, she circled, a weird
enough figure in her white draperies. The
little white feet were bare, and it taxed her
utmost strength to hold the heavy boy in
her arms, but with sublime heroism of which I should never have believed her
capable, she never once paused for breath.
A miracle alone kept the child asleep, but
when I saw the poor mother's lips move
dumbly between the strains of the gay
valse she was humming, I felt that she was
praying God that he might not waken.
Nearer and nearer the curtain she came, but
to my horror perceived that Crawford was
growing uneasy and advancing slowly in the
rear.

"Mrs. Crawford! Quick!"

There was not a minute to be lost. She tore
the curtain aside, and she rushed toward
me, but ere she could fasten the heavy door
her husband was upon us. With yell of
balled rage he was tearing after her through
the open doorway, and in another moment,
would have reached her with uplifted knife
when I tripped him up, and he fell headlong
to the floor. He was stunned by his fall
and while fastened his hands and feet by
means of the cut window cord, his wife went
back to the inner room and rang loudly for
assistance.

Ere he came to himself Arthur Crawford
was safely secured in my own room. Leav-
ing him there under charge of the men sent,
I went back to seek Mrs. Crawford.
She was lying on the bedroom floor with her
nervous fingers still tightly interlaced, and
by her side sat her little son, warm and rosy
from his broken sleep. He was kissing her
paling lips as I came hastily into the room
and now held up a warning finger as I knelt
beside them.

"Poor mamma is fast asleep," he whis-
pered. "And she is cold."

She was not dead. The long and frightful
mental strain through which she had passed
brought on brain fever, and for some days
we despaired of her life, but she came
through it bravely, and ere the summer
waned had the satisfaction of installing
both mother and son in a seaside cottage far
away from her Berkshire home.

Crawford, poor fellow, only lived a few
months, for a dangerous fall in the asylum
grounds put merciful termination to his
confinement. During those few months
I visited him occasionally, and he always
spoke most tenderly of his wife, whom
he imagined dead.

When he died I went to break the news to
his young widow, and while staying in her
pretty Devonshire cottage I solved much that
had puzzled me. Her terror at my first sight
of her had been occasioned by the
fact that she had at once recognized me;
Lennox, the mad doctor, had been pointed
out to her in the park the season before.
She dreaded Arthur's incipient madness being
known to any one, for she had been in
terror of lunatic asylum in connection
with her idolized husband, and hoped that
a quiet country life, free from trouble and
contradiction, might in time restore him. But
had he never broken out before? It
seemed to me incomprehensible that
so slight a frame should be capable of such
courage. Once, she said, only once, and
then he had been bent on killing himself;
in struggling with him for the possession
of the knife he had accidentally cut her wrist
and so occasioned the ugly scar that dis-
figured it. As for Beatrice's presence on that
fatal night, she told me he had always been
accustomed to sleep in their room and as
she had refused to second her theory that the
child wanted change of air, and so aid
sending him out of the house, she could di-
vise no other means of getting rid of him.
And then I took my leave and I have
never seen Mrs. Crawford from that day
on; but still, in spite of a certain pair
of sweet brown eyes which make the sunshine
of my home, I am forced to admit that
it is no woman on earth for whom I have such
boundless admiration as for that unfortu-
nate lady of whom at one time I thought
my first observation—Disclosures Journal.

Colonel John R. Camp was found last evening in the armory of the 22d Regiment, Fourteenth St. and Sixth Ave. Just about to take command of his regiment on the occasion of regimental drill, he said that he saw no occasion yet for apprehension in March, when matters looked threatening; he detailed a guard of a dozen to remain in the armory and hold it until the members could assemble there in case the services of the regiment were required. In his opinion, the present occasion should not require it; he would do the same thing again. In case more men had quarters in the building, it was not entirely unprotected at any time. He added that he hoped the services of the regiment would not be required, if they could be depended on to do their duty as promptly and well as they had in the past.

Colonel James Cavanagh, commander of the 69th Regiment, was at his headquarters in the armory at Tompkins Square last evening. He was regretting that any occasion should arise that would call for the services of any emergency that might arise. He saw no occasion yet for detailing guard to protect the armory, he had prepared the front to prevent it from falling into wrong hands; it had not looked threatening today, he might not do so, he thought it better not to do so unless it was deemed necessary to preserve the property.

Colonel Seward of the 11th Infantry was putting on his coat and preparing to go home from the technical building at 40th and Twenty, when services in an armory, the armory over stable, and he remarked, would take necessary precautions if others chose to attack it so. He had not detained any men for even a moment, but if trouble was serious there would be doing unless the regiment were called out. In that case we would take possession of the streets. You can see for yourself what shameful condition arises when we have appealed to the authorities to have the evil corrected. I wonder that the regiment can be kept in any decent shape, but will warrant that in case services are needed the boys will do their duty.

At the armory of the 10th Regiment, Forty-fifth St. and Broadway, several drills going on, Colonel James H. Jones said he had taken some additional precautions in view of the unsettled state of things to properly protect the armory, and he had no doubt that in case of attack the building could be held against a mob until relief arrived. SIR:—In reply to your letter of the End
inst requesting to be informed "if the
moon has anything to do with the rain,"
I have the honor to refer you to an in-
vestigation of the subject made by Prof.
Elias Loomis of Yale College, published
in the Proceedings of the American As-
sociation for the Advancement of Science,
Vol. 7, 1858, p. 80, and Vol. II, 1868, pp.
1922. These articles summarize the
results of similar European studies and
contain his own conclusions obtained
from study of the Greenwich observa-
tions. Loomis concludes that cloudi-
ness is greatest about the time of last
quarter. But others maintain that his
figures do not justify so positive state-
ment. French and English Meteorolo-
gists have more recently made contribu-
tions to this disputed question, but have
not arrived at harmonious conclusions as
to the reality of lunar influence.
It seems to be admitted however, that
the moon's heat cannot produce the
phenomena in question. M. Faye shows
that if the moon's reflected heat is in the
same proportion as the reflected light,
such heat cannot produce change of
temperature of a thousandth of degree
Fahrenheit. Lord Rosse's experiments in-
dicate that the total heat radiated and
reflected is nearly ten times the amount
of light reflected, but even with this
amount the effect must still be insensi-
ble.

shown that the heat received from the
moon is indefinitely small. This heat
cannot therefore dissipate the clouds and
whether the phenomena claimed by
Loomis and others are real relations or
phantoms, is still disputed question.

almost inappreciable in the average of
many years' observations and can have
no bearing on any question of everyday
life.

withheld when his supply was gone.

These and other circumstances reasonably, I think, led these simple people to suppose that the invitation to deposit their hard-earned savings in this institution implied an undertaking on the part of their government that their money should be safely kept for them.

When this company failed it was liable in the sum of $0,925,22 to 1,131 depositors. Dividends amounting in the aggregate to 60 per cent. have been declared, and the sum called for and paid of such dividends seems to be $1,685,157.72. This sum deducted from the entire amount of deposits leaves $1,991,744.50 still unpaid. Past experience has shown that quite a large part of this sum will not be called for. There are assets still on hand amounting to the estimated sum of $4,000. I think the remaining 35 per cent. of such of these deposits as have claimants should be paid by the government, upon principles of equity and fairness. The report of the commissioner soon to be laid before Congress, will give more satisfactory details on this subject.

The control of the affairs of the District of Columbia having been placed in the hands of purely executive officers, while the Congress still retains all legislative authority relating to its government, it becomes my duty to make known the most pressing needs of the District and recommend their consideration.

The laws of the District appear to be in an uncertain and unsatisfactory condition, and their codification or revision is much needed.

During the past year one of the bridges leading from the District to the state of Virginia became unfit for use, and travel upon it was forbidden. This leads me to suggest that the improvement of all the bridges crossing the Potomac and Anacostia branches, from the city of Washington, is worthy of the attention of Congress.

The commissioners of the District represent that the laws regulating the sale of liquor and granting licenses therefor should be at once amended, and that legislation is needed to define the scope and powers of charitable and penal institutions within the District.

I suggest that the commissioners be clothed with the power to make, within fixed limitations, police regulations. I believe this power granted and carefully guarded would tend to subserve the good order of the municipality.

It seems that trouble still exists growing out of the occupation of the streets and avenues by certain railroads having their termini in the city. It is very important that such laws should be enacted upon this subject as will secure to the railroads all the facilities they require for the transaction of their business, and at the same time protect citizens from injury to their persons or property.

The commissioners again complain that the accommodations afforded them for necessary offices for District business, and for the safekeeping of valuable books and papers, are entirely insufficient. I recommend that this condition of affairs be remedied by the Congress, and that suitable quarters be furnished for the needs of the District government.

In conclusion, I earnestly invoke such wise action on the part of the people's legislators as will subserve the public good and demonstrate during the remaining days of the Congress, as at present organized, its ability and inclination to so meet the people's needs that it shall be gratefully remembered by an expectant constituency.

GROVER CLEVELAND.

To the Editor of the Eagle.

In your response in Friday's issue on my editorial squib in the Wichita District Advocate relating to the Methodist college at Winfield, I notice an error or two which, by your permission, will correct through your columns.

1. You say: "All there was to it, and in the absence of any endowment or promised endowment, the town was asked to give the site, to give the money, and then to give the completed structure to the trustees of the conference." To this I reply, the conference did not authorize its locating committee to ask any such thing, and I know they did not ask it. The committee, representing young, but ambitious, though not wealthy conference, simply gave the different cities and towns an opportunity to bid for the location of the college. The prevailing sentiment among the leaders of the enterprise was that any city could well afford to give the site and sufficient money to construct suitable building, in view of the varied advantages naturally accruing from the location of first-class school of collegiate grade and powers. And it was further thought due the city securing the college to expend about all the money donated on the structure, and draw upon the church and its friends throughout the conference for money to defray the running expenses of the school, and in time to work up an endowment. Indeed it was well understood by the locating committee and every other person at all interested, with the possible exception of yourself, that no city would make any proposition except on the condition that the conference establish and forever maintain first class school of college grade. And everybody knows that to furnish the site and build the structure are comparatively small factors in a successful college enterprise.

2. "If the Methodist church is so destitute of funds, what is it going around and asking people to do all the work and contribute all of the money!" The Methodist church is not some great abstraction, of somewhere apart from all creation, with a huge vault full of money; it consists of intelligent men and women scattered through every city, town and country place, with willing hands and open hands to every moral, philanthropic, and intellectual enterprise. The treasurers of the church are the purses of its members, and the duly appointed agents of the church have right to call upon its members and its friends for contributions, and they have right to respond. And that is just what the Methodists did and are doing with reference to their so-called college. And we shall still continue to do it with or without the consent of the EAGLE, until our college leads every other in the state.

Very respectfully,

J. D. BOTKS

Whether young Harry Smith killed himself accidentally or intentionally at Englewood, N. J., on Tuesday night, is a question that puzzles the people of that village considerably. While the majority seem to think it of suicide, there many believe with his family that the apparent absence of any motive for such an act precludes this view. The young man's father, Charles A. Smith, was well known in business circles here. He was a member of the firm of Chapman, Smith & Britton and was in the dry goods business for over twenty years in Church Street. He retired with a snug fortune some years ago and has been living a retired life of late. His family consisted of his wife, two daughters of whom married, and Harry, who was only twenty-five years old. About four years ago Mr. Smith wanted Harry to go to college, but Harry expressing a preference for business, a position was obtained for him in the Fifth Avenue Bank. He remained there until last January, when he became tired of the work, it is said, and resigned.

Early in the spring Mr. Smith hired a cottage for the summer from William Humphries, in Englewood, and the family moved there in June. Harry stayed at home nearly all the time. The family had few acquaintances in the village and with these he and his sister were great favorites. He seemed to enjoy life greatly and on Tuesday night was in unusually high spirits. All the family slept on the second floor. They retired at 9 o'clock, as usual, but Harry told his mother when she went to kiss him goodnight, that he was well when she left him. Mr. Smith says that he had lost himself in sleep when he heard a pistol shot. At first he thought it was outside the house. He called to Harry to ask him about it, but received no reply. Knowing that Harry had a revolver, he became alarmed and with Mrs. Smith, hurried to the young man's room. There they found him gasping in the agonies of death with the blood pouring from a wound in his left side just below the heart. The revolver, a seven-shooter, lay beside him with one of the chambers empty. His left hand clutched his night shirt though he had pulled it away to uncover his breast. He was unconscious. Dr. Banks, one of the village physicians, was immediately sent for, but before he arrived the man was dead. The bullet had penetrated the lower part of the heart.

Coroner Shaw, who lives at Leon, was informed early in the morning. After examining the body he decided that it would not be necessary to hold an inquest. He considered it of suicide. "What should cause Harry to kill himself?" he asked. "He had health, wealth and everything to live for. I know positively that he had no bad habits or connections to cause trouble. When it went on an unfortunate love affair is all nonsense. He had no troubles of any kind, and was going to a party with his sister and some other friends here to-night."

About eight years ago Harry's brother, an older son, went West and bought a ranch in New Mexico in company with three or four others. He crossed into Arizona to buy cattle, but never returned from the trip. If, however, there is any one thing more than another which Virginians oppose it is the internal revenue system, with its harassing and burdensome taxation and espionage. There are many other issues upon which the difference is just as wide and manifest, but the matters cited are not only illustrative of the general antagonism between Virginia and the Democratic faith and practice, but they are controlling matters in shaping public opinion and guiding popular action, if any are. Does anybody believe that any free state and free people, holding such decided convictions as to their chief interests as the Virginia people do, would attach themselves to the Democratic party, with its record, and send such men as Barbour, Cabell, Tucker, Daniel, O'Ferrall, Trigg, and Croxton to represent them at Washington? Can anyone believe that these men recognize any allegiance or responsibility to the state and people having such convictions, seeing how they act in contempt of both? Bah! they are here in despite of Virginia and her voters, and well they know it, as their conduct proves. Tucker is announced ready to make the greatest speech of his life against the Blair bill. Bourbon Cabell, O'Ferrall, and Tucker, of the present delegation, voted for Morrison's horizontal bill. Daniel, now in the House, but United States senator-elect to represent the Bourbon usurpers, in recent speech opposing the labor arbitration bill, denounced the very moment when in his own city and all over the district he claims to represent public meetings of the people, without regard to party, were clamoring for protection, and adopting resolutions and petitions against the Morrison Hewitt free trade scheme.

The people of Virginia not only have decided convictions, such as have been cited, but they well know the Bourbons, the Democratic party, and the adverse policy pursued by these toward Virginia. Nor are they deceived by the clamor against the negro, as the vote of the white counties has persistently and increasingly shown even since 1879; still less are they fooled by the professions of the Bourbon faction. They regard these professions precisely as the mere pretexts for the outside world (as the alleged prejudice against the Republican name and the pretended fear of negro rule served so long) to explain returns and results that would otherwise be seen to be too plainly the fruit of force and fraud. Virginians also have the courage of their opinions, as their noble fight since 1879 has steadily shown. For the last three years, however, force has been too strong and fraud too swift for them; yet it is no surprise, and one worthy of all acceptance, that "the battle is not always to the strong nor the race to the swift." Many concurrent influences are working together to restore popular government in the grand old commonwealth, while Bourbonism itself is rent and betrayed by its own demoralized, disconnected, and discordant minions and mercenaries. Fairfax, in 1885, had Bourbon counted in as her delegate to the general assembly; but this delegate being rewarded by judgeship (evidently for special services rendered), the vacancy was filled only this year by the triumphant election of Republican bearing the significant name of Thorne. the distinguished people at Greystone.

ton. On the arrival of the funeral
train at New Lebanon the body was
taken to the Congregational church of
the village, where at least five thou-

offered by the Rev. Mr. Burrill, pastor
of the village church.

lines from Goethe's 'Iphigenia':


Happy, who, with a bright regard looks back
Upon his fathers' fathers, who with joy
Recounts their deeds of grace, and in himself

WASHINGTON, Aug. 1.—The spring
wheat returns to the department of
agriculture for Aug. 1 showing an im-
provement in condition in Iowa, a
small decline in Wisconsin and Ne-
braska, and heavy reduction in Da-
kota. The causes of deterioration are
drought and chinch-bugs. Heat has
been excessive in many districts that
have produced a fair yield, notwith-
standing. The harvest is two weeks
earlier than usual and the quality is
unusually good, except in sections
where heavy loss from blight has oc-
curred.


The general average of condition is
reduced from 83.2 to 80. At the time
of harvest last year the average was
86. A part of the loss last season oc-
curred after Aug. 1. As the present
harvest is already nearly over, with
improving meteorological conditions,
the final estimate cannot be much fur-
ther reduced. The present average is
81 for Iowa instead of 80 last month.
No less than twenty-five counties, each
producing from 100,000 to 1,000,000
bushels, report the condition at 100 or
over. In Minnesota there is an in-
crease from 78 to 80. The reduction in
Wisconsin is from 85 to 72, in Nebraska
from 80 to 81, and in Dakota from 85
to 81.


Winter wheat previously harvested
is not reported this month. There has
been heavy decline in the condition
of corn since the first of July. The
average, which was then 50, is reduced
to 81. The heaviest decline is in Illi-
nois.

The Sage of Nininger, however, can lay
claim to nothing but of the cipher. He
was himself a convert to the Baconian
theory, before the cipher idea dawned on
his mind and any revelations he may make
will be merely corroborative, though to a
convincing degree, of the arguments already
advanced by W. K. Smith, Delia Bacon
and others. All previous evidence so
called, is entirely circumstantial and in-
direct, but if Mr. Donnelly can prove his
position and establish the cipher, he will
not only offer direct and conclusive proof
of the Bacon authorship but will add to
history many facts concerning the Essex
instruction and perhaps shed new light
upon the queen, the "termagant Elizabeth."


WHY IT WAS NOT SHAKESPEARE


It is not at all surprising that the many
circles which have bowed so long in adora-
tion—not of the product alone, but of the
producer—should stand aghast and in
horror at the rude fall from the high
pedestal which Donnelly, et al., would give
Shakespeare. But to the world at large,
so long as the works themselves remain,
the truth concerning the authorship will
be more acceptable and not the
less so because the mighty mind
of Bacon is universally conceded
a worthy womb from which even these
matchless works might spring. An attack
upon any long-established prejudice of be-
lief will stir up antagonism and every new
discovery or invention must battle its way
to success through the ranks of skeptics, so
it is not surprising that after three centu-
ries of placid trust the attempt to dethrone
Shakespeare meets with armed opposition.


The Donnelly school of students presents,
first, reasons why Shakespeare could never
have written the works, and second, rea-
sons why Bacon, and Bacon alone, must
have done so. Some of these will epito-
mize from memory, using the arguments
quoted by Mr. Donnelly in his lecture.


He was from a poor and uneducated
and from a bookless neighborhood. His
father was "hired hand" on a neighboring
farm, and it is doubtful if he owned so
much as a family Bible. Shakespeare was
educated in school where instruction in
English was not known. Latin was the
only branch taught and in the majority of
the schools of the times, the only branch
thought worthy of being taught.
At the time of the appearance of
the first of the plays he had probably
never been beyond the precincts of his own
little precinct of Stratford, and had de-
voted his time largely to the noble pursuit
of poaching. Such was the man to whom
has been ascribed the authorship of the
grandest body of literature known to the
world. This great work was the product
of the profoundest mind of the world. Not
only must its author have been a scholar,
but a man of the highest culture and, what
was remarkable at those times, a perfect
English scholar. His acquaintance with
the classic languages must have been deep
and intimate, for the work displayed a
fluent use of new words, based upon Greek
and Latin roots and


NEVER ONCE INCORRECTLY FORMED.


Phrases and ideas were borrowed from
Italian authors never even yet translated.
Old Spanish proverbs, notably that begin-
ning, "who steals my purse steals trash,"
were coined for use; while the handker-
chief episode in "Othello" was borrowed
from an ancient Italian comedy. The
author of Shakespeare was evidently fa-
miliar with the leading cities of Italy:
and "Othello," "Merchant of Venice,"
"Romeo and Juliet," "Two Gentlemen
of Verona" and "Pericles"
could have been written only after
personal acquaintance with the scenes,
such as Shakespeare could never have had.
It was said the poem "Venus and Adonis"
was the first product of Shakespeare; that
he carried it to London in his pocket. But
in spite of the fact that this was his first
visit to the metropolis, and that he came
fresh from Warwickshire, with the local
patois on his tongue, this magnificent pro-
duction is couched in the finest, choicest
London English, without trace of pro-
vincial dialect in it. It is also shown that
Shakespeare's will contained no allusion,
whatever, to his works, though every other
possession was enumerated and disposed of.
Seven of his plays were published seventeen
years after his death, yet with these
priceless manuscripts in existence, he made
not the remotest allusion to them in his
will. One of the earlier sonnets contained
the most affectionate references to these
children of his brain, alluded to their value
and spoke of their living and talking to the
ages yet to come. The writer evidently
knew the value of the works, yet Shakes-
peare died without confiding them to the
keeping or safeguard of anybody.


Another strong point is made of the fact
that the Shakespeare plays teem with legal
knowledge and phraseology. Ex-Gov.
Davis has written a book on the Law In
Shakespeare" and similar work was pro-
duced by a Boston gentleman. It has been
remarked that when the laity resort to
legal phrases they commit blunders, but an
ancient chief justice has said: "From
Shakespeare's law there is no appeal." This
has led his commentators to the conclusion
that in early life Shakespeare read law.
But if this had been the case he would have
been in demand as a witness to various in-
struments, and the fact is that his signature
in such service is not extant.


THE EARLIEST DOUBT


Doubt cast upon the authorship was by Nash, a
contemporary, who, in 1888, complained of
certain playwrights stealing his thunder.
He says they had better stick to the trade
of lawyers, to which they were born. This
has puzzled the commentators not little.
They had agreed that Shakespeare had had
some little experience with the law, but
that it should be the trade to which he was
born could not readily be explained.
This was one of the earlier circumstances
that directed attention to Francis Bacon as
the probable author of the body of plays.
Bacon left two wills, in one of which, in
directing the publication of his works, he
referred to some that would bring greater
honor than those he had published and ac-
knowledged. The later of the Shakespeare
plays were published at the same time Ba-
con's were given to the world, in 1623.

daily papers about a week ago appeared this advertisement:

happened to meet with one of those who

"Yes," replied the woman. "I don't know anything

the paper."

"All right," was the answer, given in a demure,
serious tone of voice. "I'm not the man; I'm door-
keeper in the house of our Lord, walk in."

"What have got into him!" was the inward thought
as the woman entered; but the door opened into
a parlor and disclosed a large number of others. On the
far end she gained courage and took her seat, all
interested in the affair out there.

"Well no, I don't. I've seen it and presume it's noth-
ing I want but thought they might be looking for
a nurse in a family, perhaps some to travel with
gentle people, and thought I'd come over."

sympathetic and hearted; that he gave large sums of

begin, but he wished everyone who was not already mar-

Senator Donely hat sich als ein sehr guter Mann erwiesen. Er hat sich in den Senats-Debatten sehr engagiert gezeigt. Er hat sich für die Interessen der Bevölkerung von Washington und auch für die Tribuna eingesetzt, aber er hat dabei stets auf seine Pflichten gegenüber den Interessen der Bürger geachtet. Bis zum 1. März 1887, wenn er sein Amt niederlegt, wird er als ein sehr geschätzter Senator gelten. Er hat sich in der Gesetzgebung durch Observation-Disclosures ausgezeichnet und sich in dieser Hinsicht angefertigt. Soweit man es beurteilen kann, hat ein Senator, der die Angaben von Frauen in den Sitzungen macht, sein Amt nicht ausbezahlt werden können, weil im Senat eine Einwendung dagegen erhoben worden, dass er sein Gehalt bekommt. Zugleich hat er gegen seines unerlaubten Weglebens aus der Gemeinschaft Besogen gesprochen.

General Miles gibt die oft getuschelte Hoffnung, dass die Offiziere und Capt. Patton den grimmen und lauernden Geronimo haben, freuen Nachrichten, dass er sehr leicht zu erreichen bin. Ein Herr S. S. Gummin, welcher in Batega in Sonora ein Sergeant betreibt, und später als amerikanischer Staatsbürger des jetzigen US-Staats unter Geronimo, berichtet, dass Geronimo, als er letzte Nacht den Verlust, den er einziglich mit einem kleinen Lager nach einem hohen Gebirge, machte, 20 Meilen zurückgegangen ist, zurückgegangen habe, und dass er leer sein würde, ihm dort bekommen. Der Oberste Shell der Sarge aber befinde sich noch in der Sierra. Nun, der Lieblingsflucht der Sierras, und es scheint ein Meer nicht zu sein, um ihn aus seinen unzugänglichen Schluchten zu treiben. Cummings lässt über die See reden, und meint, selbst im einem kleinen Flotte könne der Offizier noch einmal so schnell laufen, als ein ganz früher amerikanischer Soldat.

Anfragen im Indianer-Bureau stellen, wie man dort nichts von Elmer Abbit, die Mapes der Gan Carlos Gebiet, nach Civilisierter Gegend zu erreichen. Manisten erklärt man dort, die Fortschrittlichkeit für eine lange Zeit nicht zu erreichen. Die Zahl der Mapes auf dem Gebiet beträgt 5000, wovon 5000 White Mountains, 900 Mohaves, 300 Yumas und 500 Gila River Mapes sind. Außerdem einige Duftige Überbleibsel der Santo und der Gan Carlos Stämme. Von vielen letzten es waren die Gila River, welche allein Indianer persönlich, und die gehörten eigentlich nach Dakota und liegen auf der Natur nur außerhalb, im ihren üblichen Gebieten unter dem Gebiet von Maiden. Die anderen Mapes seien friedfertig und hätten begonnen, ihr Land zu besiedeln. Von vorigen Sabre hatten die der Regierung bereits 10000 Siedler verkaufen können. Die Gila River Erbtings werde man treuende loswerden wollen; für die Besiedlung der anderen Mapes lege sei Geld vor.

Ein Kanals wird jetzt unter Leitung des Stadtplaners BRADFORD eine neue Betrieb auf eine neue Art veranstaltet, selbst in der fruchtbaren Stadt Clinton.

In St. Joseph in Missouri wurde Dr. B. u. S. nach 14 Tagen Verhandlungen von der Stadt nicht ruhig der Anordnung des Beauftragten Strong erklärt, weil er bei der Berührung der Stadt manhaftig war. Er wird in die Staats-Sitzung gebracht.

Ein Sturz in Marten County im Hillen-Siedel des mittleren Sitzes wurde dieser Sage, die bald weite und von Nachbarn angefeiert, Reise des lebendigen Mannes etc. in einem Erdloch gefunden. Der Wüter machte die Überreste der vorübergehenden Gage mit einige Wörter den Weg nach einem Picnic nach Belts Soulhaus angegangen, um dort das zu verkaufen, und erlag nämlich an einer Vergiftung. Die aufsteigenden Nasen wurden vorbeigebendet aufmerksam, somit konnte die Reise zuletzt noch lange nicht gewonnen werden.

Die Eröffnungsfahrt der "Mammut-Fahrt" hat am 11. August stattgefunden. Es waren darin Shell-Settens der preußischen Verkehrs-Oberbaurat, Settens Oberpostdirektor in Münster und für die deutsche Besiedlungs-Gehörungsrat, ferner die Mitglieder der Handelskammer von Marter, die Handelskammer Mitglieder von Schongau, München und Nürnberg, Gelgeorouter Eilgard von Witting, Hilger Meister Dieckels von Niffenburg. Utitzglieder der Generaldirektion von Niffenburg und Birstorf, die Staatsbeamte und noch eine große Gruppe Mitglieder und Gäste, im allen ca. 70 Personen. Die Teilnehmer befanden sich in einem langen, zu einem Zelt eingerichteten, reich beflaggten und mit langen Tafeln versehenen Schlafwagen, der an das Acknowledgements angeboten war. Um 1 Uhr heute ist das Schiff zwischen Berliner und den Älteren einer Tafel mit halber Kraft in die Begegnung und fuhr auch die erste Seeluft des Rheinfalls bis Dorheim, wo die Ankunft gegen 11 Uhr erfolgte. Als das Schiff eben in den Mai eingelaufen war, nahm der Vorsitzende des Aufsichtsrats, Hans Merperito Rugler von Sfeubah heraus, einen kurzen Vortrag über die Geschichte der "Mammut-Fahrt" zu geben und darauf hinweisen, wie das Unternehmen bis zu seiner Geburt mit großem Schwierigkeiten zu kämpfen gehabt habe. Das ist sicherlich auch zu Stande gekommen, lei in erster Linie den eifrigen Wirten der belgischen Regierung zu danken. Die im Verein mit Preußen und Bayern dem Unternehmen die erste Spende entgegengebracht und dessen Gründung durch Besiedlung der städtischen Wohnungen übernommen.

Special to the Journal:


WASHINGTON—It has been observed
for some time that when nominations by the
President reached the Senate the first to get
out of their seats and approach the desk of the
Vice-president to read the names, are the South
ern Senators, frequently a number of them
will rise as soon as the President's secretary
reaches the Senate to deliver the nominations,
and flock about him and prevent their announce
ment for some minutes. Inquired of a Northern
Senator the other day why this was, and he
said:


"The South is more interested at this time in
nominations of army and navy officers, and Off
icials in the consular and diplomatic service, than
any other section of the country. I never ina
gined that such keen interest would be felt, but
it is true, and observe it especially in the con
sideration of these nominations in committees
and in secret sessions of the Senate.


Why do you think this is true?" asked.


"In the first place," replied the Senator,
Southern people have very inflated ideas of
the importance of the army and navy, and of
our representatives abroad. Secondly, they are
just now looking ahead to continuation of the
administration, and they believe these officers
have great power in keeping in existence any ad-
ministration. You remember the South made
great disturbance over the alleged interference
of the army at the polls a number of years ago,
and then it was taught to reverence and fear it.
Ever since that time there has been growth of
respect for at least the army, and it is but nat
ural that the diplomatic officers should be re-
garded highly, since they have much to do at
times in maintaining peace or bringing about
war. The South is the most aggressive, if not
the most enterprising part of our country, and
anything in the line of chivalry or diplomacy in
terests that section intensely."

the sheriff declared them elected with-
out calling for any difference in
opinion, but if there was an excess of
